sections.text:
The whole camp is crying, and it goes on all night. The spies have come back with a fearful report, and the people cry out, “We wish that we had died in the land of Egypt,” they say. Two of the spies, Joshua and Caleb, tear their clothes and plead with them. The land, they say, is “an exceedingly good land”. But the crowd threatens to stone them.

That night in chapter 14 is the center of Numbers. The book follows Israel from Mount Sinai to the edge of the promised land, a journey that takes about forty years. It opens with a census and marching orders, and then tells of complaints, rebellion and unbelief. After the spies’ report, the generation that left Egypt is told it will die in the wilderness. Yet even then God says that he will bring in their little ones, “they shall know the land which you have rejected.”

The book ends with a new generation camped on the plains of Moab, counted again and ready to enter the land.

The English name comes from the two censuses in chapters 1 and 26. The Hebrew title means in the wilderness, which describes the book better. The very large numbers of people are debated. Some take them at face value, while others think the Hebrew word translated thousand may mean a clan or a military unit.

The New Testament uses these stories as both warning and encouragement, most clearly in 1 Corinthians 10 and Hebrews 3 and 4. The bronze serpent of chapter 21 is the picture Jesus uses of his own death in John 3.

Readers also notice how patient God is in this book. Judgment falls, and still he keeps the promise and brings the people on.

A people who walked out of slavery are now counted like an army. It is the second year after Egypt, in the wilderness of Sinai, and the LORD tells Moses to take a census of every man twenty years old and up who can go to war. One head from each tribe stands with Moses and Aaron, and the names are given: Elizur, Shelumiel, Nahshon and nine more.

Then the numbers roll out tribe by tribe. Reuben is counted at 46,500, Judah at 74,600, Dan at 62,700. The total is 603,550.

One tribe is left out. The LORD tells Moses not to count Levi. The Levites are set over the tabernacle, to carry it, care for it and camp around it, so that no wrath falls on the people. The chapter ends with Israel doing all that was commanded.

The book of Numbers takes its English name from these censuses. Israel has been at Sinai since Exodus 19, and now the camp is being organized for the march to the land. Many scholars debate how the large numbers should be understood, and the text itself does not explain them. The setting apart of the Levites ties to the laws of Leviticus. Christians and Jews read the lists as a record of every tribe and name being known to God.

Picture a camp arranged like a great square around the tabernacle. The LORD tells Moses and Aaron that each tribe must camp under its own standard, at some distance from the Tent of Meeting. On the east, toward the sunrise, stand Judah, Issachar and Zebulun. On the south are Reuben, Simeon and Gad. On the west are Ephraim, Manasseh and Benjamin. On the north are Dan, Asher and Naphtali.

Each group has its prince and its numbers, and each camp's total is given: 186,400 for Judah's camp, 151,450 for Reuben's, 108,100 for Ephraim's, 157,600 for Dan's. When the camp moves, they march in order: Judah first, Reuben second, then the Tent of Meeting with the Levites in the middle, then Ephraim, and last Dan. The Levites are not counted among the other tribes. Israel does just as the LORD commanded.

The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron, and this chapter shows how the tribes were to camp and march. It follows the census of Numbers 1. The Tent of Meeting stands at the center, so the camp is built around the presence of God. Many readers see in the order a sign that the people were not a crowd but a community with a place for everyone. The same order is repeated when they set out in Numbers 10.

The chapter starts by naming Aaron's four sons, and then it recalls a loss: Nadab and Abihu died before the LORD when they offered strange fire in the wilderness of Sinai, and had no children. Eleazar and Ithamar carry on.

Then the LORD makes a claim. He has taken the Levites from among Israel in place of all the firstborn, because on the day he struck the firstborn in Egypt he made every firstborn in Israel holy to himself. Moses counts the Levites by their three families, Gershon, Kohath and Merari, every male a month old and up: 22,000 in all. Each family gets a place to camp around the tabernacle and a share of its work.

Then the firstborn of Israel are counted: 22,273. For the 273 who exceed the Levites, Moses collects five shekels apiece, and gives the money to Aaron and his sons.

The LORD speaks to Moses at Sinai. This chapter explains why the tribe of Levi serves at the sanctuary: they stand in place of the firstborn, who belonged to God after the exodus; see Exodus 13. The deaths of Nadab and Abihu are told in Leviticus 10. Many readers note that the arithmetic of the 273 shows the redemption was carried out exactly. The role of the Levites is later echoed in the New Testament, for example in Hebrews 7.

Someone has to carry the holy things, and this chapter says exactly who and how. The LORD tells Moses and Aaron to count the men of each Levite family from thirty to fifty years old. The sons of Kohath carry the most holy things, but they may not touch them or look on them. Aaron and his sons go in first when the camp moves, covering the ark with the veil and a cover of sealskin and a blue cloth. The table, the lamp stand and the altars are each wrapped in their own cloth.

Only then do the Kohathites come to carry, “lest they die.” The Gershonites carry the curtains and hangings. The Merarites carry the boards, bars, pillars and sockets. Counts follow for each family: 2,750, 2,630 and 3,200, 8,580 in all.

The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron in the wilderness. The chapter is a work assignment for the Levites when the tabernacle moves, and it shows how seriously the holy things are treated: the Kohathites are protected by the rule that they must not see or touch them. Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron's sons, supervise. In Numbers 7 the Merarites and Gershonites receive wagons. Christians have often read the care taken here as a picture of reverence before God.

The camp has a center, and the LORD dwells in it, so the chapter begins with a cleansing of the camp. Those with a skin disease, a discharge or uncleanness from a corpse are sent outside, and Israel does it. A person who wrongs another must confess and repay in full, adding a fifth.

Then comes a hard case. A husband feels the spirit of jealousy, though there is no witness. He brings his wife to the priest with an offering of barley. The priest has her stand before the LORD, loosens her hair, and gives her holy water mixed with dust from the floor of the tabernacle, with a curse written and washed into it. She says “Amen, Amen.” If she is guilty, her body will swell and her thigh fall away. If she is innocent, she is free and will conceive.

The LORD speaks to Moses. The first part ties to the laws of Leviticus 13 to 15. The second part, often called the ordeal of jealousy, is one of the hardest in the Bible: only the wife is tested, and the text gives no matching rite for a husband. Many scholars see it as a way to protect a woman from violence by handing the case to God, since no human witness is available. Christians and Jews read it differently. For another case involving a woman accused, see John 8.

Some people in Israel set themselves apart for a time, and this chapter describes the vow. A man or woman may take a Nazirite vow to be separate to the LORD. For the days of the vow they drink no wine or strong drink, eat nothing from the grapevine, let no razor touch their head, and go near no dead body, not even for a father or mother. If someone dies suddenly nearby, the head is shaved and offerings are made, and the days start again.

When the days are done, the Nazirite comes to the Tent of Meeting with a lamb, a ewe lamb, a ram and a basket of bread. The hair is shaved and burned on the fire of the peace offering.

The chapter ends with words still used in worship: “The LORD bless you, and keep you.”

The LORD speaks to Moses, and then tells Aaron and his sons how to bless Israel. The Nazirite vow is open to both men and women. Samson, in Judges 13, and Samuel, in 1 Samuel 1, are linked to similar vows, and Paul takes a vow in Acts 18. The blessing at the end is thought to be among the oldest pieces of text still in common use. Jews and Christians both use it in worship, and the LORD says it puts his name on his people.

The tabernacle is finished, anointed and made holy, and the leaders of Israel come with gifts. The twelve princes bring six covered wagons and twelve oxen. The LORD tells Moses to accept them and give them to the Levites. Gershon receives two wagons and four oxen, Merari four wagons and eight oxen. Kohath gets none, since their duty is to carry the holy things on their shoulders.

Then, for twelve days, one prince each day brings the same offering for the altar: a silver platter of 130 shekels, a silver bowl of 70, a golden ladle of ten shekels full of incense, and a long list of animals. The chapter names each prince and each day, and repeats the gift every time. In the end the totals are added up. The chapter closes quietly: Moses goes into the Tent, and he hears the LORD speaking to him from above the mercy seat.

This is the longest chapter in the first half of Numbers, and its repetition has a purpose: every tribe is named and every gift is counted, so that none is forgotten or placed above another. The chapter looks back to the setting up of the tabernacle in Exodus 40. The wagons ease the work of the Levites described in Numbers 4. The last verse shows the purpose of it all, that God speaks to Moses from the mercy seat.

First, light. The LORD tells Moses to say to Aaron that when he lights the lamps, the seven lamps shall give light in front of the lamp stand. Aaron does so. The lamp stand is of beaten gold, made on the pattern the LORD showed Moses.

Then the Levites are cleansed for service. Water of cleansing is sprinkled on them, they shave their whole bodies, wash their clothes, and are presented before the Tent with the whole congregation gathered. The people lay their hands on the Levites, and Aaron offers them as a wave offering. The Levites then lay their hands on the heads of two bulls, one for a sin offering and one for a burnt offering. The LORD says again that he has taken them in place of the firstborn.

After that they serve. The Levites begin at twenty-five and retire from the work at fifty, but still assist their brothers.

The LORD speaks to Moses. This chapter completes the setting apart of the Levites begun in Numbers 3, and the age for service differs from the thirty given in Numbers 4. Many readers think the difference reflects different kinds of work or a later practice, and the text does not settle it. The lamp stand recalls Exodus 25. The laying on of hands shows that the people themselves present the Levites to God. See Hebrews 7 for how the priesthood is read later.

A year after leaving Egypt, the LORD tells Israel to keep the Passover, and they do, in the wilderness of Sinai. But some men are unclean from touching a dead body, and they come to Moses and Aaron with a question: “Why are we kept back” Moses does not answer on his own. He says, “Wait, that I may hear what the LORD will command”.

The LORD gives a second chance. Anyone unclean or far away on a journey may keep the Passover one month later. But the person who is clean and nearby and simply fails to keep it is cut off. A foreigner who wishes to keep it may, under one statute.

The chapter then turns to the cloud over the tabernacle. When it rests, Israel camps, whether two days, a month or a year. When it lifts, they travel.

The LORD speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. The Passover is described in Exodus 12, and this is the first time it is kept after the exodus. The men's question leads to a new rule, a pattern seen elsewhere in Numbers when people bring a case before Moses. The cloud of fire and smoke shows how Israel was guided; compare Exodus 40. Many readers see in the closing verses a picture of trust, moving and resting at God's word.

Two silver trumpets are made, and they become the voice of the camp. Blown together, they call the whole congregation to the Tent of Meeting. One alone calls the princes. An alarm sends the eastern camps forward, and a second alarm the southern. The priests, Aaron's sons, blow them, and in war the sound will make Israel remembered before the LORD.

On the twentieth day of the second month in the second year, the cloud lifts, and Israel leaves Sinai for the first time. Judah goes first, then the others in the order set earlier. Moses asks his father-in-law Hobab to come along: “you can be our eyes.” Hobab says he will go home.

The ark goes ahead three days' journey. When it moves, Moses says, “Rise up, LORD,” and when it rests, “Return, LORD, to the ten thousands of the thousands of Israel.”

The LORD speaks to Moses, and the camp leaves Sinai, where Israel had stayed since Exodus 19. The marching order follows Numbers 2. The text does not say whether Hobab finally went; compare Judges 1 for a hint about his family. Moses' words over the ark are the best known part of the chapter, and are still prayed in some synagogues when the Torah scroll is carried. The march begins in order and hope, and the next chapter shows how quickly it frays.

The march is only days old when the complaints start. The people grumble in the LORD's ears, and fire burns at the edge of the camp until Moses prays. Then the hunger for meat begins. They weep: “Who will give us meat to eat?” They remember fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic. All they have is manna.

Moses is at the end of himself. “I am not able to bear all this people alone”. The LORD tells him to gather seventy elders, and takes some of the Spirit on Moses and puts it on them. They prophesy. Two men, Eldad and Medad, prophesy in the camp. Joshua wants them stopped, but Moses says, “I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets”.

Then the LORD sends quails. The people gather them greedily, and a plague strikes while the meat is still between their teeth.

The LORD speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Paran region, soon after leaving Sinai. The manna was first given in Exodus 16. This chapter shows leadership under strain: Moses asks to die, and God shares the burden among seventy elders. Moses' wish that all God's people be prophets is echoed in Joel 2 and Acts 2, where Christians see it fulfilled at Pentecost. The place names mark the cost: the text says they buried the people who lusted.

The trouble this time comes from inside Moses' own family. Miriam and Aaron speak against him because of the Cushite woman he had married. Then the real complaint comes out: “Has the LORD indeed spoken only with Moses? Hasn’t he spoken also with us?” The text adds a quiet aside: Moses was very humble, more than all others on earth.

The LORD calls the three of them to the Tent of Meeting and comes down in a pillar of cloud. He tells Aaron and Miriam that prophets receive visions and dreams, but with Moses he speaks mouth to mouth, plainly. When the cloud lifts, Miriam is leprous, white as snow.

Aaron pleads with Moses, and Moses cries out, “Heal her, God, I beg you!” She is shut outside the camp seven days, and the people wait for her before moving on.

The LORD speaks to Moses, Aaron and Miriam. The text does not say who the Cushite woman was, and readers have disagreed about it for centuries. The chapter is mainly about the place of Moses among the prophets, and Hebrews 3 later calls him faithful in God's house. Miriam's role as a prophet is noted in Exodus 15. The people's waiting for her shows she was valued. Some readers see in Moses' prayer a pattern of intercession.

They are almost there. At Paran, on the edge of Canaan, the LORD tells Moses to send men to spy out the land, one leader from each tribe. The names are given, among them Caleb of Judah and Hoshea of Ephraim, whom Moses calls Joshua. Moses sends them with a list: Is the land good or bad? Are the people strong or weak? Are the cities camps or strongholds? “Be courageous,” he says, and bring some fruit.

They go the length of the land. At the valley of Eshcol they cut a single cluster of grapes so large that two men carry it on a staff. After forty days they return. The land flows with milk and honey, they say, but the people are strong and the cities fortified. Caleb says to go up at once. The others say, “We aren’t able” They saw the Nephilim, and felt like grasshoppers.

The LORD speaks to Moses, and the spies set out from the wilderness of Paran, near Kadesh. The land had been promised to Abraham, as in Genesis 15. The men give a report of fact, then a report of fear, and the text calls the second an evil report. The chapter sets up the crisis of Numbers 14. Deuteronomy 1 retells the story from Moses' own view. Christians have often read this story as a warning about unbelief; see Hebrews 3.

The people cry all night. They say they wish they had died in Egypt, and they decide to choose a leader and go back. Moses and Aaron fall on their faces. Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes and plead: the land is exceedingly good, and “the LORD is with us.” The crowd talks of stoning them, and the glory of the LORD appears at the Tent.

The LORD says he will strike them and make of Moses a greater nation. Moses pleads instead, appealing to what the LORD himself has said: slow to anger, abundant in loving kindness. The LORD pardons, yet the generation that refused will not enter the land. They will wander forty years, a year for each day of the spying. Caleb will go in. Their children will go in.

The people then try to attack anyway, without the ark, and are beaten back to Hormah.

The LORD speaks to Moses at Kadesh in the wilderness of Paran. This is a turning point in Numbers, since it explains why Israel spent forty years in the wilderness. Moses' prayer uses the words the LORD spoke about himself in Exodus 34. Psalm 95 and Hebrews 3 and 4 look back on this event as a warning. The text holds both forgiveness and consequence together, and Christians and Jews have both reflected on how they fit.

After the failure at Kadesh, the LORD speaks of a future: “When you have come into the land” The chapter gives rules for offerings made there, with fine flour, oil and wine measured out for each lamb, ram and bull. One law is to apply to the native-born and to the foreigner alike. The first of the dough is to be given as a wave offering.

There is a difference between sin done unwittingly, which can be atoned for with an offering, and sin done “with a high hand,” which despises the LORD's word and brings being cut off.

Then a man is found gathering sticks on the Sabbath. He is held in custody, since no ruling has been given. The LORD says he must be stoned outside the camp, and it is done. The chapter ends with a gentler command: put blue-corded fringes on your garments, so you may see them and remember.

The LORD speaks to Moses, and this chapter looks past the forty years toward life in the land. The Sabbath had been commanded in Exodus 20 and 31. The case of the man gathering sticks is hard, and the text does not explain why his act is treated as a defiant one. The fringes, called tzitzit by Jews, are still worn, and Jesus' clothing is mentioned in Matthew 9 and Matthew 23. Christians read these laws in different ways.

Korah, a Levite, gathers 250 respected leaders and stands before Moses and Aaron. “You take too much on yourself, since all the congregation are holy”. Moses falls on his face. He tells Korah to bring censers with fire and incense to the LORD the next day, and the LORD will show who is holy. Dathan and Abiram refuse to come at all, and accuse Moses of making himself a prince.

The next day the glory of the LORD appears. Moses and Aaron plead for the people. Then the ground splits open and swallows Korah's household and goods alive, and fire consumes the 250. The people flee.

But by morning the congregation says, “You have killed the LORD’s people!” A plague begins. Aaron runs into the crowd with incense and stands between the dead and the living, and the plague stops.

The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron, and this revolt tests the special place of the priests and of Moses. Korah's complaint sounds like a call for equality, and Moses answers that they seek the priesthood too. Many scholars see more than one complaint woven together here: one by Levites, one by Reubenites. Jude 11 mentions Korah as a warning. Christians and Jews read the story as being about the holiness of God and the danger of presumption.

The LORD answers the quarrel about the priesthood with a sign. Moses is to collect a rod from each tribe's leader, twelve in all, and write each man's name on his rod. On the rod of Levi, Aaron's name. They are laid before the covenant in the Tent. The rod of the man the LORD chooses will bud.

The next morning Moses goes in. Aaron's rod has sprouted, budded, produced blossoms, and borne ripe almonds, all in a single night. Moses brings all the rods out, and each man takes his own.

The LORD says to put Aaron's rod back before the covenant, as a token against rebellion, so that the complaining will end and the people not die. But the people are afraid: “Behold, we perish! We are undone!” Everyone who approaches the tabernacle dies, they say, and ask if they will all perish.

The LORD speaks to Moses, and this chapter ends the dispute begun in Numbers 16. The rod is kept as a lasting sign; Hebrews 9 mentions Aaron's rod that budded as being kept with the ark. The people's fear shows how heavy the experience of the holy has become for them, and the next chapters give the priests and Levites a duty to guard the sanctuary. Christians have often seen in the budding rod a sign of life from what seemed dead.

After the rebellion and the budding rod, Aaron hears a sobering word: he and his sons will bear the weight of the sanctuary. The priesthood is a gift, and it is also a danger. The Levites are given to Aaron as helpers, but they may not come near the vessels of the sanctuary or the altar, or both they and the priests would die.

Then the chapter turns to provision. The priests receive a share of the offerings, the first fruits of oil, wine and grain, and the redemption price for the firstborn, set at five shekels. The firstborn of cows, sheep and goats are not redeemed but offered. It is called a covenant of salt.

The priests get no land. The LORD tells Aaron that he himself is their portion and inheritance. The Levites receive the tithe, and they in turn give a tithe of the tithe to the priests.

The LORD is speaking mostly to Aaron, and near the end to Moses, in the wilderness after Korah's challenge to the priesthood and the sign of Aaron's rod (see Numbers 16 and 17). Israel has just feared that anyone who comes near the Tent will die. This chapter answers that fear by spelling out who serves, who keeps watch, and how those who serve are fed. Compare the Levites' lot in Deuteronomy 10 and the tithe laws in Leviticus 27.

Death is the great stain in this chapter, and God provides a way to be made clean from it. The people are to bring a red heifer without defect, one that has never worn a yoke. Eleazar the priest takes her outside the camp, where she is killed and burned. Cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet are thrown into the fire. Everyone who handles the sacrifice is unclean until evening, and they must wash.

A clean man gathers the ashes and stores them outside the camp. Mixed with running water, they become the water for impurity.

The rest of the chapter deals with touching a body, a bone or a grave. That person is unclean seven days, and is sprinkled on the third and seventh days. Anyone who refuses defiles the LORD's tabernacle and is cut off from Israel.

The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron in the wilderness, in a camp where thousands have recently died (see Numbers 16 and 17). Death is everywhere, and the Tent of Meeting stands at the center of the camp. The chapter shows how the community could live near a holy place and still bury its dead. Hebrews 9 refers back to this ritual, and Christians and Jews have read its meaning in different ways.

The chapter opens with a grave. Israel reaches Kadesh, and Miriam dies there and is buried. Then the water runs out, and the people turn on Moses and Aaron with bitter words about Egypt and the wilderness.

Moses and Aaron fall on their faces, and the LORD's glory appears. They are told to take the rod, gather the people, and speak to the rock. Moses stands before the assembly and says, “Hear now, you rebels!” He strikes the rock twice, and water comes out abundantly. But the LORD tells both brothers that they did not believe in him enough to honor him before the people, and they will not bring this assembly into the land.

Edom refuses Israel passage, and Israel turns away. At Mount Hor, Aaron's garments are placed on his son Eleazar, Aaron dies on the mountain, and all Israel weeps for thirty days.

Most scholars and the tradition place these events near the end of Israel's forty years in the wilderness. The people are a new generation, but their complaint echoes the one at Rephidim (see Exodus 17). Moses is the leader under strain, and the loss of Miriam and Aaron marks the end of an era. Readers have long asked exactly what Moses' failure was, and Jewish and Christian interpreters offer several answers.

A string of short stories carries Israel toward the edge of the land. A Canaanite king captures some Israelites, and Israel vows to destroy his cities. The place is named Hormah.

Then the people grow discouraged on the long way around Edom. They speak against God and Moses and complain of the food. The LORD sends venomous snakes, and many die. The people confess, and Moses prays for them. The LORD tells him to make a snake and set it on a pole, and everyone who looks at it lives.

The journey continues with a well and a song: “Spring up, well!” Israel asks Sihon of the Amorites for passage and is refused, and Israel defeats him and settles in his cities. Og of Bashan comes out to battle next. The LORD says not to fear him, and there are no survivors.

These stories belong to the closing years of the wilderness journey, as Israel moves up the east side of the Dead Sea toward the Jordan. The chapter quotes older songs, including The Book of the Wars of the LORD, which the text itself names. In John 3 Jesus points back to the bronze snake, and Christians read the connection in different ways. The battle accounts are hard reading and have been debated for centuries.

Moab is afraid. Israel has camped on its plains, and King Balak has seen what Israel did to the Amorites. He sends for Balaam, a man whose blessing and curse are believed to work, and offers him honor.

Balaam asks the messengers to wait the night. God tells him not to go and not to curse the people, because they are blessed. Balak sends more princes, and more honorable ones. Balaam says that even a house full of silver and gold cannot move him beyond the word of the LORD. This time God says to go, but only to speak what he is told.

On the road the donkey sees the LORD's angel with a sword drawn, and Balaam cannot. She turns, presses against a wall, and lies down, and Balaam strikes her three times. Then the LORD opens her mouth. Balaam's eyes are opened, and he bows. He is told to go on, but to speak only what he is given.

The scene is the plains of Moab across the Jordan from Jericho, near the end of the wilderness years. Israel is only a presence here; the story is told from the side of Moab and a foreign prophet. Why God's anger burns after he told Balaam to go has long puzzled readers, and interpreters differ. Later writers remember Balaam differently, as in Joshua 24 and 2 Peter 2.

On a high place of Baal, Balaam builds seven altars, and a bull and a ram are offered on each. He goes off alone to meet God, and the LORD puts a word in his mouth. Balak, the king, stands waiting beside his offering.

The word is not a curse. Balaam says, “How shall I curse whom God has not cursed?” He sees a people who dwell alone, too many to count, and he asks to die the death of the righteous. Balak is furious. He says he asked for a curse and got a blessing.

Balak tries another place, the top of Pisgah, with seven more altars. Again the word is a blessing: God is not a man, that he should lie, and what he has blessed Balaam cannot reverse. A third attempt at Peor is begun as the chapter ends.

Balak is a king of Moab, afraid of the people camped on his border, and Balaam is a seer brought from far away. The poems here are some of the oldest-sounding verse in the Torah, and the sayings that God does not lie or repent are often quoted in discussions of God's faithfulness. Compare 1 Samuel 15, where a similar line appears in another setting. Christians and Jews read the chapter as a picture of a blessing that cannot be bought away.

By now Balaam has stopped looking for omens. He turns his face toward the wilderness, sees Israel camped tribe by tribe, and the Spirit of God comes on him.

He speaks as a man whose eyes are open, who hears the words of God and sees the vision of the Almighty. His poem is full of beauty: tents, valleys, gardens by a river, cedars beside the waters. Israel is a lion that lies down, and who will rouse it? Whoever blesses Israel is blessed, and whoever curses is cursed.

Balak strikes his hands together in anger, tells Balaam to go home, and says that the LORD has kept him from honor. Balaam answers that he said all along he could say only what the LORD says. He speaks once more, of a star that will come out of Jacob and a scepter from Israel, and gives short sayings about Edom, Amalek, the Kenites and Asshur. Then both men go their ways.

This is the last of Balaam's sayings, spoken near the end of the wilderness years while Israel is encamped on the plains of Moab. Many Jewish and Christian readers have heard in the star and scepter a royal promise, and some link it to David and some to the Messiah. Scholars and traditions differ on how far the poem looks ahead. Compare Genesis 49 and Matthew 2.

The chapter begins with a failure. Israel is staying at Shittim, and the people are drawn into the worship of the daughters of Moab's gods. They eat, they bow down, and Israel joins himself to Baal Peor. The LORD's anger burns, and a plague begins.

Moses is told to deal with the chiefs, and the judges are to put to death those who joined themselves to Baal Peor. While the people weep at the door of the Tent of Meeting, a man of Israel brings a Midianite woman into the camp in front of everyone. Phinehas, the grandson of Aaron, takes a spear and kills them both. The plague stops, but twenty-four thousand have died.

The LORD gives Phinehas a covenant of peace and an everlasting priesthood, and tells Moses to harass the Midianites.

The setting is Shittim on the edge of the promised land, with the wilderness generation almost gone. Later writers recall this event as a warning: see Numbers 31, Deuteronomy 4, Psalm 106 and 1 Corinthians 10. The passage is violent, and it has been misused to justify taking violence into one's own hands. Jewish and Christian readers differ on how to understand Phinehas' act and what it asks of anyone today.

After the plague, the LORD tells Moses and Eleazar the priest to count the people again, from twenty years old and up, everyone able to go to war. It is a roll call tribe by tribe, family by family. Reuben, Simeon, Gad, Judah and the rest are named, and the totals are given. The grand total is six hundred one thousand seven hundred thirty.

Three small notes break up the lists. Dathan and Abiram, who rebelled with Korah, are named, and the text adds that the sons of Korah did not die. Zelophehad had no sons but five daughters, and each is named. And the land is to be divided by lot, in proportion to the numbers.

The chapter ends with the Levites, counted separately, and a stark verdict: of those counted at Sinai, not one remained except Caleb and Joshua.

This is the second census in Numbers. The first was taken at Sinai (see Numbers 1), and this one comes at the plains of Moab, at the very edge of the land. A whole generation has passed. The numbers prepare for the division of the land in Joshua. Whether the figures are meant literally or in another way is debated, and scholars hold several views.

Five sisters walk up to the door of the Tent of Meeting. Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah stand before Moses, Eleazar, the princes and the whole congregation. Their father died in the wilderness and had no sons. Why should his name disappear from his family? They ask for a possession among their father's brothers.

Moses brings their cause before the LORD, and the answer is clear: the daughters of Zelophehad speak right. A new rule follows for the whole people. A man's inheritance passes to his daughter if he has no son, then to his brothers, then to his father's brothers, then to the nearest kinsman.

Then the LORD tells Moses to go up the mountain of Abarim and see the land he will not enter. Moses asks for a shepherd for the people. Joshua, a man in whom is the Spirit, is commissioned.

These scenes take place on the plains of Moab, shortly after the second census. The daughters come forward because the land is about to be divided and they would receive nothing. Their case returns in Numbers 36 and in Joshua 17. The second half of the chapter looks toward Moses' death and prepares for Joshua to lead. Compare Deuteronomy 31 and 34.

The chapter is a calendar of offerings, laid out day by day and season by season. The LORD wants his offering brought in its due season.

Every day there are two lambs, one in the morning and one at evening, with flour, oil and a drink offering. The Sabbath adds two more lambs. At the start of each month there are two young bulls, a ram, seven lambs and a goat for a sin offering.

Then come the feasts. Passover falls on the fourteenth day of the first month, and the Feast of Unleavened Bread follows for seven days, with a holy gathering on the first and seventh days and no regular work. The day of first fruits, in the feast of weeks, has its own offering too.

The amounts are exact, down to the tenths of an ephah of flour, and every animal must be without defect.

Moses is passing on commands the LORD gave, here to the new generation about to enter the land. Most of these offerings were first described in Exodus 29 and Leviticus 23. This chapter gathers them into one schedule so that worship would have a steady rhythm. Christians and Jews read these sacrificial laws differently, and the New Testament speaks of them in Hebrews 10.

The calendar of offerings continues into the seventh month, the busiest month of Israel's year. On the first day there is a day of blowing of trumpets, with a holy gathering and no regular work.

On the tenth day the people are told to afflict their souls and do no kind of work. Offerings are made, including a sin offering of atonement. This is the day later known as the Day of Atonement.

On the fifteenth day a feast to the LORD begins, and it lasts seven days. The offerings on this feast are the largest of the year, beginning with thirteen young bulls, and the number of bulls drops by one each day: twelve, eleven, ten, down to seven. On the eighth day there is a solemn assembly with one bull. These come on top of vows and free will offerings.

These are further instructions from the LORD through Moses, given to the people on the plains of Moab. The seventh month holds the trumpets, the day of afflicting souls, and the feast known in other places as Tabernacles (see Leviticus 23). Jewish tradition still marks these days, and Christians read their meaning in Hebrews 9 and 10 in different ways. The chapter closes the calendar begun in Numbers 28.

This chapter is about words that bind. Moses speaks to the heads of the tribes: when a man vows a vow to the LORD, he must not break his word. He must do all that comes out of his mouth.

Then the chapter turns to the vows of women, and it is a hard section to read today. A young woman in her father's house, or a wife in her husband's house, makes a vow. If her father or husband hears it and says nothing on the day he hears, the vow stands. If he forbids it that day, it does not stand, and the LORD will forgive her. The vows of a widow or a divorced woman stand against her. A husband who cancels a vow after the day has passed bears her iniquity.

The chapter closes by calling these the statutes between a man and his wife and between a father and his daughter.

Moses is giving the tribal heads instructions on the plains of Moab, in a society where fathers and husbands held legal authority over households. The text speaks of the culture of its time and some readers see protection in the rules, while others see a limit on women's agency. Christians and Jews read it with care and differ about its present meaning. For the weight of vows more generally, see Deuteronomy 23 and Ecclesiastes 5.

This is one of the hardest chapters in the book. The LORD tells Moses to avenge Israel on the Midianites, and afterward Moses will be gathered to his people. A thousand men from each tribe go out with Phinehas, carrying the vessels of the sanctuary and the trumpets. They kill every male, including five kings and Balaam son of Beor. The women and children are taken captive, and the cities are burned.

Moses is angry with the officers for sparing the women, who he says caused Israel's trespass at Peor. He orders the killing of every male child and every woman who has known a man, and says the girls who have not may be kept alive.

The soldiers and the captives must be purified. The plunder is counted and divided, and a portion goes to the LORD. The officers bring gold as an offering to make atonement for their souls.

The chapter looks back to the Midianites' part in the plague at Peor (see Numbers 25) and is Moses' last act before his death. It is war law and war account together. Readers have struggled with it for centuries, and the numbers are read by some as literal and by others as symbolic. Passages like this have been misused to justify violence against peoples today, which most Jewish and Christian traditions firmly reject.

Reuben and Gad come to Moses with a request. Their herds are huge, and the land east of the Jordan, Jazer and Gilead, looks like good country for livestock. They ask to settle there and not cross the river.

Moses answers sharply. Shall your brothers go to war while you sit here? He reminds them of the spies at Kadesh Barnea, whose fear discouraged the whole people, and of the forty years that followed. He warns that they may do the same again.

The two tribes make a counter offer. They will build sheepfolds and cities for their little ones, but their armed men will go ahead of the others until every tribe has its land. Moses agrees on one condition: keep your word, or be sure your sin will find you out.

He gives the land to Gad, Reuben and half of Manasseh, and the tribes begin to build and rename the towns.

The scene is the plains of Moab on the eastern side of the Jordan, with the conquest of Sihon and Og behind them (see Numbers 21). The question is one of loyalty: will two tribes settle comfortably while the rest still fight? Moses' fear is rooted in what happened at Kadesh in Numbers 13 and 14. The agreement is recalled in Deuteronomy 3 and in Joshua 1 and 22.

Moses wrote down the starting points of Israel's journeys by the commandment of the LORD, and this chapter is that record. It begins at Rameses on the fifteenth day of the first month, the day after the Passover, when Israel went out with a high hand while the Egyptians buried their firstborn.

Then comes the list, stop by stop. Succoth, Etham, the sea, Marah, and Elim, where there were twelve springs and seventy palm trees. Rephidim, where there was no water. Sinai. Kibroth Hattaavah. Kadesh. Mount Hor, where Aaron died at the age of one hundred twenty-three. On and on, until the camp stands in the plains of Moab by the Jordan.

The chapter ends with a charge for what lies ahead: drive out the inhabitants, destroy their idols, divide the land by lot. If Israel fails to do so, those who remain will be like pricks in the eyes.

This is a travel diary in the form of a list, written from the vantage of Israel's last camp before the Jordan. It covers about forty years. Some of its places match stories told in Exodus and Numbers, and others appear only here. Many scholars are unsure where some of the sites lay. The closing charge is repeated in Deuteronomy 7 and Judges 2.

The LORD draws the map of the promised land in words. He tells Moses to say to the people: when you come into the land of Canaan, this is the land that shall fall to you for an inheritance.

The south border runs from the wilderness of Zin along Edom, from the end of the Salt Sea, past Kadesh Barnea toward the brook of Egypt and the sea. The west border is the great sea. The north border runs by Mount Hor toward the entrance of Hamath, and the east border runs down toward the sea of Chinnereth and along the Jordan to the Salt Sea.

Then the leaders are named. Eleazar the priest and Joshua will divide the land, and one prince from each tribe will help. Caleb represents Judah. Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh have already received their share across the Jordan.

The people are still in the plains of Moab, and the boundaries given here are a promise before they are a fact. Many of the place names are no longer certain, and scholars debate the exact line. The list of leaders matters because the generation that left Egypt is gone, and Caleb is the one survivor named from it (see Numbers 14). The actual division of the land is told in Joshua 13 to 19.

The Levites will have no land of their own, so the LORD tells Moses to give them cities to live in. Forty-eight cities, with pasture lands measured out around each one, will come from the other tribes, more from the large tribes and fewer from the small.

Six of those cities are cities of refuge. A person who kills someone unwittingly may flee there from the avenger and stand before the congregation for judgment. The refuge is for the stranger and the foreigner too.

The law draws a line. A man who kills with an iron tool, a stone, a wooden weapon, or out of hatred or lying in wait is a murderer and must die. A killing without hostility is judged differently, and the one who killed must stay in the city of refuge until the high priest dies. No one may be put to death on one witness alone. The chapter ends by saying blood pollutes the land, and the LORD dwells among the people.

The Levites' lack of an inheritance goes back to Numbers 18. The cities of refuge are placed in the setting of an age when family members carried out justice, and this law slows that cycle and puts a court between the killer and the avenger. The refuges are set out again in Deuteronomy 19 and Joshua 20. The ban on ransom for murder shows how seriously the text treats a human life.

The story of the daughters of Zelophehad is not quite finished. The heads of the family of Gilead come to Moses with a worry. If the daughters marry men from other tribes, their inheritance will pass to those tribes and be taken away from the tribe of Manasseh. Even the jubilee would not give it back.

Moses says that the tribe of the sons of Joseph speak what is right. The LORD commands that the daughters may marry whomever they think best, only within the family of their father's tribe. In this way no inheritance moves from one tribe to another, and each tribe keeps its own.

The daughters do as the LORD commanded. Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah and Noah marry sons of their father's brothers, and their inheritance stays in the tribe.

The last verse closes the whole book.

This chapter follows the ruling in Numbers 27 and tests it. The setting is still the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, just before the crossing. The concern is that tribal land stay in the tribal family. The daughters appear again in Joshua 17, where they receive their share. The book ends here, with Israel at the border and the commands of the LORD in hand.
